TOOL RESULT: # Writing Effective AGENTS.MD Files: Key Recommendations

## What Works

**Specificity Over Vagueness**
The analysis of 2,500+ repositories revealed that successful agent files define specialists, not generalists. As the article states, "You are a test engineer who writes tests for React components" outperforms "You are a helpful coding assistant."

**Six Core Areas to Cover**
1. Commands (with flags and options)
2. Testing frameworks
3. Project structure
4. Code style examples
5. Git workflow
6. Boundaries

**Command Placement**
Put executable commands early: `npm test`, `pytest -v`, `npm run build`. Include specific flags rather than just tool names.

**Concrete Examples**
One real code snippet demonstrating your style beats lengthy explanations. Show what good output looks like.

**Three-Tier Boundaries**
Structure rules as:
- ✅ Always do
- ⚠️ Ask first  
- 🚫 Never do

## Structure & Content

**What to Include (Bare Minimum):**
- One-sentence project description
- Package manager specification (if non-npm)
- Non-standard build/typecheck commands

That's it. As the guide emphasizes, "the ideal `AGENTS.md` file should be as small as possible."

**What to Exclude:**
- Redundant instructions agents already know
- Vague or obvious guidelines
- File system structure documentation (too prone to staleness)
- Auto-generated content from initialization scripts

## Progressive Disclosure Strategy

Rather than cramming everything into one file, distribute guidance across a hierarchical system:

- **Root level**: Only truly universal information
- **Separate domain files**: Language-specific rules, testing patterns, API conventions
- **Nested documentation**: Create discoverable resource trees agents can navigate when needed

## What Makes a Good AGENTS.md

**Effective patterns:**

1. **Progressive disclosure** - Keep the main file to 100-150 lines with focused reference documents agents load on-demand. Longer files see diminishing returns.

2. **Procedural workflows** - Step-by-step numbered instructions move agents from failure to completion. One six-step deployment workflow improved correctness by 25% and completeness by 20%.

3. **Decision tables** - Resolve ambiguity before coding. Tables comparing "React Query vs Zustand" improved best practices scores by 25%.

4. **Real code examples** - Short 3-10 line snippets from production code boost reuse by 20%, but more than a few causes pattern-matching errors.

5. **Pairing "don'ts" with "dos"** - "Don't instantiate HTTP clients directly. Use the shared apiClient from lib/http instead" outperforms warnings alone.

## Structure & Organization

AGENTS.md files should follow a hierarchical approach with **global guidance** in `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (shared defaults) and **project-specific rules** in repository roots. Use nested `AGENTS.override.md` files for directory-specific customizations that supersede broader instructions.

## Length & Content Guidelines

Keep combined instruction files under the default **32 KiB limit** (`project_doc_max_bytes`). Prioritize high-impact guidance:

- Working agreements and team norms
- Testing and linting requirements  
- Dependency management policies
- Security-sensitive procedures

As the documentation notes: *"Codex concatenates files from the root down, joining them with blank lines."* Place critical rules closer to your working directory since later files override earlier ones.

content.text:
Read 6 sources. Summary + audit of your AGENTS.md below.

## What guides say

**1. [GitHub blog — lessons from 2,500+ repos](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-to-write-a-great-agents-md-lessons-from-over-2500-repositories/):** Specificity wins. Lead with executable commands (exact flags). One real code snippet beats paragraphs of description. Structure boundaries three-tier: ✅ always / ⚠️ ask first / 🚫 never. Top failure: abstract rules without examples.

**2. [Augment Code — good vs bad AGENTS.md](https://www.augmentcode.com/blog/how-to-write-good-agents-dot-md-files):** Keep main file **100–150 lines**; use progressive disclosure (details in reference docs loaded on demand). 30+ warning rules = "overexploration trap," output quality drops up to 30%. Numbered step-by-step workflows improved correctness 25%. Pair every "don't" with a "do."

**3. [AI Hero — complete AGENTS.md guide](https://www.aihero.dev/a-complete-guide-to-agents-md):** "Ideal AGENTS.md is as small as possible." Frontier LLMs follow **~150–200 instructions** with reasonable consistency — every rule past that degrades all of them. Test for each line: "relevant to every single task?" If no, move to separate file. Cut what models already know. Stale docs poison context.

**4. [OpenAI Codex AGENTS.md guide](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md):** Hierarchical layering (global → repo → nested). Prioritize high-impact: working agreements, test/lint requirements, security. Verify the agent actually loaded instructions by asking it to summarize them.

**5. [Lakera prompt engineering guide](https://www.lakera.ai/blog/prompt-engineering-guide):** Ambiguity and **competing/duplicate instructions** are top causes of non-compliance. Structure with headers/delimiters. Demonstrate via examples, not abstract description.

**6. [2026 prompting roundups](https://sarifulislam.com/blog/prompt-engineering-2026/) ([IBM](https://www.ibm.com/think/prompt-engineering)):** Few-shot examples king for consistent format. Calm direct instructions beat aggressive ones — "CRITICAL!", "NEVER EVER", wall-of-bold **hurts** newer Claude models.

## Audit of your AGENTS.md

It's well-organized, but it violates the biggest findings. Why agent veers off every five messages:

1. **Way over instruction budget.** ~320 lines, 20 rules × ~6 sub-bullets ≈ 120+ directives before cross-references. Right at/over the ~150–200 ceiling — model triages and silently drops rules. This is the #1 cause of drift.

2. **Heavy duplication = competing instructions.** "Record in journal.md" appears in ~12 rules. Scope discipline stated in Rules 5, 10, 11, 12, 15, 20, and order-of-operations. E2E required in Rules 4, 14, 19, 20. Repetition doesn't reinforce — it dilutes and makes the model treat all rules as boilerplate.

3. **Emphasis inflation.** Bold **never/must/zero** in nearly every bullet. When everything is critical, nothing is. Calm direct phrasing follows better on current Claude models.

4. **No executable commands.** Guides say lead with literal commands; file references `make test`, `ruff`, `mypy --strict` abstractly but the project has no Makefile, no `docs/functions.md`, no `tests/` yet — instructions about nonexistent artifacts = stale-context poison from day one.

5. **No few-shot examples** except journal template (which is good — that's the part most likely to be followed). `docs/functions.md` entry, commit message, "good vs bad name" need one literal example each.

6. **Three overlapping checklists** (per-rule self-checks + Rule 20 + Order of Operations). Pick one.

7. **Process overhead causes drift itself.** "Read journal.md completely" + "journal very frequently" + commit-per-unit + doc-prune-per-response eats huge context every session — less room for the actual task, more veering.

## Recommended restructure

- **Shrink root to ~120 lines.** Keep: order-of-operations, three-tier boundary table (✅ always / ⚠️ ask / 🚫 never), exact commands, journal template pointer.
- **Progressive disclosure:** move rule detail to `docs/rules/` files referenced by name ("Before writing tests, read docs/rules/testing.md") — agents load on demand, near-100% follow-through for direct references.
- **Deduplicate:** each constraint stated exactly once. One checklist.
- **Create the referenced artifacts now** (Makefile, `docs/functions.md`, `journal.md`, `tests/`) or instructions stay aspirational.
- **One literal example each** for doc entry, commit message, journal entry.
- **Drop all-bold tone**; plain imperatives.
- **Cap journal read:** "read last 20 entries + skim TL;DRs of rest" — full-file reads will blow context as journal grows, guaranteeing drift.

Want me restructure file along these lines?

Sources: [GitHub blog](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-to-write-a-great-agents-md-lessons-from-over-2500-repositories/), [Augment Code](https://www.augmentcode.com/blog/how-to-write-good-agents-dot-md-files), [AI Hero](https://www.aihero.dev/a-complete-guide-to-agents-md), [OpenAI Codex](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md), [Lakera](https://www.lakera.ai/blog/prompt-engineering-guide), [sarifulislam.com](https://sarifulislam.com/blog/prompt-engineering-2026/), [IBM](https://www.ibm.com/think/prompt-engineering)
